prompt: Why does the section say a real surface can't be treated as perfectly flat when studying chemisorption and physisorption?

choices.text: Its cavities, ridges and edges behave differently
Its atoms are arranged just as in the bulk
choices.why: The section's point is the opposite: a surface's structure differs from the bulk's, with features the bulk lacks.

choices.text: Gases adsorb only on perfectly flat regions
choices.why: Nothing restricts adsorption to flat regions. The cavities, protrusions, ridges and edges are sites in their own right and must be treated differently.

choices.text: A surface is flat only at high temperature
choices.why: The section ties roughness to no temperature. Few, if any, surfaces are perfectly flat, so their features must be treated separately.

explanation: Few, if any, surfaces are perfectly flat. The kinetics and thermodynamics of processes on a surface depend greatly on its structure, so cavities, protrusions, ridges and edges must be treated differently from flat regions.

prompt: Figure 31.9.1 labels the defects on a solid surface. What is an adatom?

choices.text: A lone single atom sitting on a terrace
A missing atom that leaves a cavity
choices.why: That is a vacancy. An adatom is the opposite case: a lone extra atom on top of a terrace.

choices.text: An atom at the corner of a step edge
choices.why: That position is a kink in the step. An adatom is a lone single atom sitting on a terrace.

choices.text: An atom buried just below the surface
choices.why: An adatom is added on top of the surface, not hidden below it. It is a lone single atom on a terrace.

explanation: The surface is built of terraces, ledges, kinks and steps. Terraces can carry adatoms, lone single atoms on top of them, and vacancies, missing atoms that leave cavities.

prompt: In the section's picture of a solid surface, what is a vacancy?

choices.text: A missing atom that leaves a cavity
A lone single atom on a terrace
choices.why: That is an adatom, an extra atom. A vacancy is a missing atom, which leaves a cavity in the terrace.

choices.text: The drop from one terrace to the next
choices.why: That is a step. A vacancy is a single missing atom that leaves a cavity in a terrace.

choices.text: A flat region with no defects at all
choices.why: That describes an ideal terrace. A vacancy is a defect in it: a missing atom that leaves a cavity.

explanation: Figure 31.9.1 shows terraces that can contain adatoms (lone single atoms) and vacancies (missing atoms that leave cavities). Both are defects that make a real surface differ from a flat ideal plane.

prompt: The section introduces two forms of electron microscopy for surfaces. What does each one map?

choices.text: SEM the topography, SAM the composition
SEM the composition, SAM the topography
choices.why: The roles are swapped. SEM images the topography with secondary electrons; SAM maps composition with the Auger electrons of one element.

choices.text: Both map the composition of the surface
choices.why: Only SAM is element specific, through characteristic Auger electrons. SEM gives a direct image of the surface topography.

choices.text: Both give the atomic positions in the cell
choices.why: Atomic positions come from quantitative LEED. SEM images topography and SAM maps composition, at nanometre resolution.

explanation: Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) gives a direct image of the surface topography from the emitted secondary electrons. Scanning Auger microscopy (SAM) forms compositional maps from the Auger electrons emitted by a particular element.

prompt: A chemist wants an image showing where palladium sits on a catalyst surface. Which technique from the section gives that kind of map?

choices.text: Scanning Auger microscopy
Scanning electron microscopy
choices.why: SEM contrast comes mainly from topography, not from which element is present. SAM images the Auger electrons characteristic of one element.

choices.text: Qualitative LEED
choices.why: Qualitative LEED gives the size, symmetry and alignment of the adsorbate unit cell, not an image of where an element sits. SAM gives compositional maps.

choices.text: Quantitative LEED with I-V curves
choices.why: I-V curves give atomic positions in an ordered structure, not a map of where an element is. SAM maps composition.

explanation: SAM forms its image from the Auger electrons emitted by a particular element, and Auger energies are characteristic of the element. So it gives a compositional map, showing where that element is on the surface.

prompt: What probe beam do SEM and SAM both use, according to the section?

choices.text: A focused beam of 10–50 keV electrons
A focused beam of 20–200 eV electrons
choices.why: That low energy range belongs to LEED. SEM and SAM focus a beam of high-energy electrons, typically 10–50 keV.

choices.text: A broad, unfocused 10–50 keV beam
choices.why: The energy is right, but the beam must be focused: focusing is what gives SEM and SAM their spatial localization.

choices.text: A focused beam of X-ray photons
choices.why: Both are electron microscopies. The probe is a focused beam of high-energy electrons, typically 10–50 keV.

explanation: Both techniques focus a probe beam of high-energy electrons, typically 10–50 keV, onto a small spot. Focusing gives spatial localization: the signal comes from where the beam lands, so scanning the beam builds an image.

prompt: When the SEM primary beam strikes the surface, electrons with a wide range of energies are emitted. Which kind makes up the vast majority?

choices.text: Secondary electrons from inelastic scattering
Backscattered primary electrons
choices.why: Backscattered primaries are emitted, but they are a minority. Most are secondary electrons formed in multiple inelastic scattering processes.

choices.text: Auger electrons from ionized atoms
choices.why: Auger electrons are emitted too, but they are few; SAM is resolution limited because its signal is weak. Most electrons are secondaries.

choices.text: Elastically scattered electrons
choices.why: Elastic scattering is what LEED uses for its pattern. In SEM, the bulk of the emitted electrons are secondaries from multiple inelastic scattering.

explanation: The emitted electrons include backscattered primaries and Auger electrons, but the vast majority are secondary electrons formed in multiple inelastic scattering processes. SEM records their current to form its image.

prompt: The secondary electrons that SEM uses to form its image play what role in Auger spectroscopy, according to the section?

choices.text: They are background and are ignored
They carry the element-specific signal
choices.why: The element-specific signal is the Auger electrons. The secondaries contribute only background, which Auger spectroscopy ignores.

choices.text: They form the diffraction pattern
choices.why: Diffraction patterns belong to LEED, and there only elastic electrons count. In Auger spectroscopy, secondaries are background.

choices.text: They set the energy of the Auger peaks
choices.why: Auger energies are set by the relaxation of the ionized atom, characteristic of the element. Secondaries are just background.

explanation: The secondary electrons formed in multiple inelastic scattering contribute to the background and are completely ignored in Auger spectroscopy. The same electrons that are noise there are the signal in SEM.

prompt: What, according to the section, is an SEM micrograph a plot of?

choices.text: Secondary electron current against probe position
Secondary electron current against beam energy
choices.why: Varying the beam energy is how LEED I-V curves are made. SEM keeps the energy fixed and records the current as the beam scans across the surface.

choices.text: Auger electron current against probe position
choices.why: That is how SAM forms its compositional map. SEM records the secondary electron current at each probe position.

choices.text: Diffracted beam intensity against angle
choices.why: That describes a diffraction measurement, not a microscope image. SEM records the secondary electron current at each beam position.

explanation: As the primary beam is scanned across the surface, the secondary electron current I reaching the detector is recorded. The image is a plot of I against probe position on the surface.

prompt: Contrast in an SEM micrograph arises from several mechanisms. Which one does the section put first and foremost?

choices.text: Variations in surface topography
Variations in elemental composition
choices.why: Composition is what SAM maps, using Auger electrons. SEM contrast comes first and foremost from topography.

choices.text: Variations in the surface unit cell
choices.why: The unit cell is what LEED probes through diffraction. SEM contrast comes mainly from the shape of the surface.

choices.text: Variations in the beam energy
choices.why: The beam energy is fixed while the image is recorded. Contrast comes mainly from variations in topography.

explanation: The contrast arises first and foremost from variations in surface topography. That is why the secondary electron micrograph is virtually a direct image of the real surface structure.

prompt: What limits the resolution of SEM, according to the section?

choices.text: Beam spot size and scattering in the substrate
The need to collect enough Auger signal
choices.why: That is the main extra limit on SAM. SEM's secondary signal is plentiful; its limit is the beam's spot size and its scattering in the substrate.

choices.text: The de Broglie wavelength of 20–200 eV electrons
choices.why: Those wavelengths matter for LEED diffraction. SEM uses 10–50 keV electrons, and its resolution is set by spot size and scattering.

choices.text: The need for a single-crystal sample
choices.why: A single crystal is a requirement of LEED, not a resolution limit of SEM, which images any surface's topography.

explanation: The resolution is limited by the minimum spot size of the incident electron beam and, ultimately, by the scattering of the beam as it interacts with the substrate. Modern instruments reach better than 5 nm.

prompt: Modern SEM resolves better than 5 nm. For which sample does the section call that insufficient?

choices.text: Many supported metal catalysts
Semiconductor device structures
choices.why: The section calls 5 nm more than adequate for imaging semiconductor devices. It is many supported metal catalysts that need finer detail.

choices.text: Adhesive droplets on a Post-it note
choices.why: Figure 31.9.2 shows these imaged well by SEM. The section calls 5 nm insufficient for many supported metal catalysts.

choices.text: Any surface with terraces and steps
choices.why: The section names no such limit for stepped surfaces in general. It says 5 nm is insufficient to study many supported metal catalysts in detail.

explanation: A resolution better than 5 nm is more than adequate for semiconductor device structures. It is insufficient to study many supported metal catalysts in any detail, since their features are smaller still.

prompt: How does the SAM primary beam produce the Auger electrons that form the image?

choices.text: It ionizes atoms, which emit them as they relax
It diffracts off the ordered surface lattice
choices.why: Diffraction is the LEED process. In SAM the primary electrons ionize atoms, and the ionized atoms emit Auger electrons as they relax.

choices.text: It loses energy in many inelastic collisions
choices.why: Multiple inelastic scattering makes the secondary electrons that SEM uses. Auger electrons come from the relaxation of ionized atoms.

choices.text: It is reflected back toward the detector
choices.why: Reflected primaries are backscattered electrons. Auger electrons come from atoms that the beam has ionized, as they relax.

explanation: The incident primary electrons ionize atoms in the illuminated region. The ionized atoms then relax and emit Auger electrons whose energies are characteristic of the elements present, which is what makes SAM element specific.

prompt: SAM's resolution is rarely better than about 15–20 nm, worse than SEM's. What extra limit does the section blame?

choices.text: Collecting enough Auger signal in reasonable time
A much larger spot from a lower-energy beam
choices.why: SAM uses the same kind of focused 10–50 keV beam as SEM. Its extra limit is gathering enough Auger signal for an image in reasonable time.

choices.text: Auger electrons that diffract off the lattice
choices.why: Diffraction plays no part in SAM. The limit is that the Auger signal is weak, so a decent image takes time to acquire.

choices.text: Having to use a single-crystal sample
choices.why: That is a requirement of LEED. SAM's extra limit is collecting enough Auger signal to form an image in a reasonable time.

explanation: As in SEM, the resolution is ultimately limited by the beam. More significantly, enough Auger signal must be acquired to form a respectable image in a reasonable time, so the resolution is rarely better than about 15–20 nm.

prompt: Features 10 nm across need to be imaged. Going by the resolutions the section quotes, which microscope can resolve them?

choices.text: SEM, but not SAM
SAM, but not SEM
choices.why: That reverses the two. SEM resolves better than 5 nm; SAM is rarely better than about 15–20 nm.

choices.text: Both SEM and SAM
choices.why: SEM can (better than 5 nm), but SAM is rarely better than about 15–20 nm, coarser than 10 nm features.

choices.text: Neither SEM nor SAM
choices.why: SEM resolves better than 5 nm, so 10 nm features are within its reach. Only SAM, at about 15–20 nm, falls short.

explanation: Modern SEM achieves better than 5 nm, so 10 nm features are resolved. SAM, limited by the need to collect enough Auger signal, is rarely better than about 15–20 nm, so it cannot.

prompt: In qualitative LEED, only the positions of the diffraction spots are analysed. What do they reveal?

choices.text: The size, symmetry and alignment of the adsorbate cell
The exact positions of the atoms in the cell
choices.why: Atomic positions need the quantitative method: intensities measured against beam energy (I-V curves) and compared with theory.

choices.text: Which elements are present on the surface
choices.why: LEED is a diffraction technique, not an elemental one; composition maps come from SAM. Spot positions give the adsorbate unit cell's geometry.

choices.text: A direct image of the surface topography
choices.why: That is what SEM gives. LEED records a diffraction pattern, whose spot positions describe the adsorbate unit cell.

explanation: Analysing the spot positions yields the size, symmetry and rotational alignment of the adsorbate unit cell with respect to the substrate unit cell. Finding the atomic positions within it needs the quantitative I-V method.

prompt: What is an I-V curve in quantitative LEED?

choices.text: A beam's intensity against incident electron energy
Secondary electron current against probe position
choices.why: That is how an SEM image is built. An I-V curve follows the intensity of a diffracted beam as the incident beam energy changes.

choices.text: Sample current against the voltage on the grids
choices.why: The grids only filter out the slower secondary electrons. An I-V curve is a diffracted beam's intensity against incident electron energy.

choices.text: Spot position against the angle of incidence
choices.why: The beam is incident normally, and spot positions are the qualitative data. I-V curves record intensities as the beam energy varies.

explanation: In the quantitative method the intensities of the diffracted beams are recorded as a function of incident electron beam energy, giving I-V curves. Comparing them with theoretical curves can give accurate atomic positions.

prompt: How does quantitative LEED arrive at accurate atomic positions on a surface?

choices.text: By comparing measured I-V curves with theoretical ones
By reading them straight off the spot positions
choices.why: Spot positions give only the size, symmetry and alignment of the unit cell. Atomic positions come from comparing measured and theoretical I-V curves.

choices.text: By imaging the atoms with secondary electrons
choices.why: That is SEM, which resolves about 5 nm at best, far coarser than atomic positions. LEED compares measured I-V curves with theory.

choices.text: By mapping each element's Auger electrons
choices.why: That is SAM, which maps composition at 15–20 nm. LEED gets atomic positions by fitting measured I-V curves with theoretical ones.

explanation: The diffracted beam intensities are recorded as a function of beam energy to give I-V curves. Comparing these with theoretical curves for trial structures can give accurate information on atomic positions.

prompt: What kind of sample does LEED require, according to the section?

choices.text: A single crystal with a well-ordered surface
A powder with many randomly oriented grains
choices.why: Random grains do not give one ordered surface for the electrons to diffract from. LEED needs a single crystal with a well-ordered surface.

choices.text: Any surface, ordered or disordered
choices.why: A diffraction pattern needs a periodic arrangement to scatter from. The sample must be a single crystal with a well-ordered surface.

choices.text: A thin film that the beam passes through
choices.why: LEED records a back-scattered pattern, not a transmitted one. The sample must be a single crystal with a well-ordered surface.

explanation: The sample must be a single crystal with a well-ordered surface structure to generate a back-scattered electron diffraction pattern. Without long-range order there are no sharp diffracted beams.

prompt: What electron beam does a LEED experiment use?

choices.text: A well-defined energy of 20–200 eV, incident normally
A well-defined energy of 10–50 keV, incident normally
choices.why: 10–50 keV is the high-energy beam of SEM and SAM. LEED is low-energy electron diffraction, at about 20–200 eV.

choices.text: A well-defined energy of 20–200 eV, at a grazing angle
choices.why: The energy is right, but the section has the beam incident normally on the sample.

choices.text: A broad spread of energies, incident normally
choices.why: The beam has a well-defined energy, which is needed for a sharp pattern and for I-V curves. It is typically 20–200 eV.

explanation: LEED uses a beam of electrons of a well-defined low energy, typically 20–200 eV, incident normally on the sample. The back-scattered electrons form the diffraction pattern on a fluorescent screen.

prompt: Which electrons form the LEED pattern on the fluorescent screen, and how are the others kept out?

choices.text: Elastic ones; grids filter out the slower secondaries
Secondary ones; grids filter out the elastic electrons
choices.why: That is reversed. Only elastically scattered electrons diffract into the pattern; the lower-energy secondaries are removed by the grids.

choices.text: Elastic ones; the screen absorbs the secondaries
choices.why: The right electrons, but the wrong filter. Energy-filtering grids placed in front of the screen remove the secondaries.

choices.text: Auger ones; grids filter out all of the others
choices.why: Auger electrons are the signal in SAM, not LEED. The LEED pattern is made by elastically scattered electrons.

explanation: Only the elastically scattered electrons contribute to the diffraction pattern. The lower-energy secondary electrons are removed by energy-filtering grids placed in front of the fluorescent screen that displays the pattern.

prompt: By the Bragg equation, what must be true of the electrons' de Broglie wavelength λ for diffraction from planes a distance d apart?

choices.text: λ < 2d
λ > 2d
choices.why: The inequality is reversed. Electrons whose wavelength exceeds 2d cannot be diffracted by planes d apart; λ must be less than 2d.

choices.text: λ < d/2
choices.why: That is far stricter than needed. The section's condition is λ < 2d, twice the distance between the atomic planes.

choices.text: λ = d exactly
choices.why: No exact match is required. Any wavelength less than 2d, twice the plane spacing, allows diffraction.

explanation: The section states that the de Broglie wavelength must be less than 2d, twice the distance between the atomic planes. Since λ falls as the accelerating potential rises, this sets a minimum voltage for diffraction.

prompt: Using λ = ((1.504 V nm^2)/φ)^(1/2), what is the de Broglie wavelength of electrons accelerated through φ = 37.6 V, in nm?
explanation: λ = (1.504 V nm^2 / 37.6 V)^(1/2) = (0.0400 nm^2)^(1/2) = 0.200 nm. This is comparable to the spacing between atomic planes, which is why low-energy electrons diffract from surfaces.

prompt: Electrons are accelerated through φ = 100 V, so λ = ((1.504 V nm^2)/φ)^(1/2). Using the condition λ < 2d, what is the smallest interplanar spacing d, in nm, that can diffract them?
explanation: λ = (1.504 V nm^2 / 100 V)^(1/2) = 0.1226 nm. Diffraction needs 2d > λ, so d > λ/2 = 0.0613 nm. Planes closer together than this cannot diffract electrons of this energy.

prompt: With λ = ((1.504 V nm^2)/φ)^(1/2), the accelerating potential is raised from 30 V to 120 V. What is the ratio λ_new/λ_old? (Give it as a decimal.)
explanation: λ ∝ φ^(−1/2), so λ_new/λ_old = (30/120)^(1/2) = (1/4)^(1/2) = 0.5. Quadrupling the potential halves the wavelength.

prompt: Electrons accelerated through 20 V strike a crystal whose atomic planes are 0.120 nm apart. Using λ = ((1.504 V nm^2)/φ)^(1/2) and λ < 2d, are they diffracted?

choices.text: No: λ = 0.274 nm, more than 2d = 0.240 nm
Yes: 20 V lies within the usual LEED range
choices.why: Being in the typical 20–200 eV range doesn't guarantee diffraction. Here λ = 0.274 nm exceeds 2d = 0.240 nm, so these electrons are not diffracted.

choices.text: Yes: λ = 0.274 nm, less than 2d = 0.480 nm
choices.why: That doubles the spacing twice. 2d = 2 × 0.120 nm = 0.240 nm, which is less than λ = 0.274 nm, so there is no diffraction.

choices.text: Yes: λ = 0.0752 nm, less than 2d = 0.240 nm
choices.why: 0.0752 nm^2 is λ^2, before taking the square root. λ = 0.274 nm, which exceeds 2d = 0.240 nm, so there is no diffraction.

explanation: λ = (1.504 V nm^2 / 20 V)^(1/2) = (0.0752 nm^2)^(1/2) = 0.274 nm, while 2d = 0.240 nm. Since λ > 2d, there is no diffraction; a higher accelerating potential is needed to shorten λ below 0.240 nm.
